name.text: What does it mean when a parabola and a line do not intersect?

questiontext.text:
The graphs of the following two equations are drawn on the grid.

\[ \color{red}{ {#eq1tex#} } \qquad \text{and} \qquad \color{blue}{ {#eq2tex#} } \] [[jsxgraph width="560px" height="560px"]] var board = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, { boundingbox: [-8.8, 8.8, 8.8, -8.8], axis: false, grid: false, keepaspectratio: true, showCopyright: false, showNavigation: false, pan: {enabled: false}, zoom: {enabled: false} }); /* labelled square grid, one line per whole number */ var gi; for (gi = -9; gi != 10; gi++) { board.create('line', [ [gi, 0], [gi, 1] ], {strokeColor: '#d4d4d4', strokeWidth: 1, fixed: true, highlight: false, layer: 0}); board.create('line', [ [0, gi], [1, gi] ], {strokeColor: '#d4d4d4', strokeWidth: 1, fixed: true, highlight: false, layer: 0}); } board.create('axis', [ [0,0], [1,0] ], {strokeColor: '#222222', strokeWidth: 2, ticks: {ticksDistance: 1, insertTicks: false, minorTicks: 0, majorHeight: 10}}); board.create('axis', [ [0,0], [0,1] ], {strokeColor: '#222222', strokeWidth: 2, ticks: {ticksDistance: 1, insertTicks: false, minorTicks: 0, majorHeight: 10}}); board.create('text', [8.6, 0.5, 'x'], {fixed: true, anchorX: 'right', fontSize: 16}); board.create('text', [0.3, 8.6, 'y'], {fixed: true, anchorY: 'top', fontSize: 16}); board.create('text', [-0.12, -0.1, '0'], {fixed: true, anchorX: 'right', anchorY: 'top', fontSize: 12}); var aa = ({#aa#}), pp = ({#pp#}), qq = ({#qq#}), mm = ({#mm#}), nn = ({#nn#}); var parab = board.create('functiongraph', [function(t) { return aa * t * t + pp * t + qq; }, -8.8, 8.8], {strokeColor: '#c62828', strokeWidth: 3, fixed: true, highlight: false}); var L1 = board.create('point', [0, nn], {visible: false, withLabel: false, name: ''}); var L2 = board.create('point', [1, mm + nn], {visible: false, withLabel: false, name: ''}); var ln = board.create('line', [L1, L2], {strokeColor: '#1565c0', strokeWidth: 3, fixed: true, highlight: false}); [[/jsxgraph]]

(a) Look carefully at the two graphs. What does this tell you about the solutions of the simultaneous equations?

generalfeedback.text:
What “solving simultaneous equations” means on a graph. A solution is a pair \( (x, y) \) that makes both equations true at once. A point on the red curve satisfies the first equation and a point on the blue line satisfies the second, so a solution is a point that lies on both graphs: an intersection point. The number of intersection points is the number of solutions.

var dLin = Math.abs(y - mm * x - nn) * v / Math.sqrt(1 + Math.pow(mm * v / u, 2)); return Math.min(dPar, dLin, Math.abs(x) * u - 18, Math.abs(y) * v - 18, (8.8 - Math.abs(x)) * u, (8.8 - Math.abs(y)) * v); return Math.min(clearAt(cx, cy), clearAt(cx - 34 / board.unitX, cy), clearAt(cx + 34 / board.unitX, cy)); }); var bt = cands[sc.indexOf(Math.max.apply(null, sc))]; board.create('text', [mx + 64 * Math.cos(bt) / board.unitX, my + 64 * Math.sin(bt) / board.unitY, 'gap = {#gaptxt#}'], {anchorX: 'middle', anchorY: 'middle', fontSize: 14, fixed: true, highlight: false}); [[/jsxgraph]]

Reading this graph. The red curve \( {#eq1tex#} \) and the blue line \( {#eq2tex#} \) never touch or cross. The green segment marks where the vertical gap between them is smallest: at \( x={@xs@} \) it is still {#gaptxt#} units, and everywhere else it is bigger. A gap that never becomes zero means there is no point on both graphs, so the simultaneous equations have no real solution. (They are called inconsistent: no values of \( x \) and \( y \) make both equations true together.)

Why the part of the plane we cannot see does not matter. The grid shows only a small part of the plane, so we confirm with algebra that the graphs never meet anywhere. At an intersection both equations give the same \( y \), so set the two expressions equal:

\[ {#rhs1#} = {#rhs2#} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad {#quad#} = 0. \]

A quadratic equation \( ax^2+bx+c=0 \) has real solutions only if its discriminant \( b^2-4ac \) is not negative. Here \( a={@aa@},\ b={@cq@},\ c={@cr@} \), so

\[ b^2-4ac = ({@cq@})^2-4({@aa@})({@cr@}) = {@dd@} < 0. \]

The discriminant is negative, so the equation has no real roots: there is no real \( x \) at which the curve and the line meet, and therefore no real solution to the simultaneous equations.

Why the other options in (a) are wrong. “Exactly one solution” would need the line to just touch the curve (a tangent), but here there is always a gap. “Two solutions” would need the line to cut the curve twice. “Infinitely many” would need the two graphs to be the same. And a solution cannot be hiding outside the picture, because the algebra above shows that the graphs do not meet anywhere on the plane.

Part (b). The true statements are: no point satisfies both equations; the quadratic obtained by equating the two expressions has a negative discriminant (no real roots); and the equations are inconsistent. The line is not a tangent (a tangent would touch the curve once), and extending the grid would not make the graphs meet.

node.description: closest point mistaken for a solution

truefeedback.text: The place where the graphs are closest is not a solution. A solution must lie on both graphs, and here there is still a gap between them.
Two solutions would mean that the line crosses the curve in two places. Look again: do these graphs cross anywhere?
Infinitely many solutions would need every point of one graph to lie on the other, i.e. the two equations would describe the same graph. A parabola and a line are never the same graph.
The graphs do not meet anywhere on the plane, not only inside the picture. (The worked solution shows why using algebra.)
Almost: exactly one of the statements is classified wrongly (a true statement left out, or a false one ticked). Think again about what it means for a point to be a solution.

falsefeedback.text: Several of the statements are classified wrongly. Remember: a solution is a point that lies on both graphs. Do these graphs have any point in common?

qtest.description: Radio: closest point mistaken for a solution
